title: Restore justice
hook: restore our judges as at first

segments.voice: Yesterday, the great shofar and the scattered people. Your line was gather the scattered. Did you make a plan with someone far away? Today, once the people are gathered, the question of who judges them. Day five hundred eighty-eight.

Most people have had at least one experience of a system that didn't work. A landlord who ignored the law. A boss who promoted the friend. A court case that dragged on for years and ended up with the side that had more money. The feeling is very specific: not just that something went wrong, but that the place you were supposed to go when things go wrong was broken too. The eleventh blessing of the Amidah is a prayer about exactly that place.
screen: `A SYSTEM THAT DIDN'T WORK.` → `THE PLACE YOU GO, BROKEN TOO.` → `THE ELEVENTH BLESSING.`

segments.voice: It says: restore our judges as at first, and our counselors as at the beginning. Remove from us sorrow and sighing. Reign over us, You alone, with kindness and compassion, and vindicate us in judgment. Blessed are You, King who loves righteousness and justice. The first line is lifted almost word for word from Isaiah. In the old Jewish translation: "And I will restore thy judges as at the first, and thy counsellors as at the beginning." Isaiah is speaking to a Jerusalem whose leaders, he says, love bribes and ignore the orphan and the widow. The repair he imagines isn't a new system. It's a return to the old one working the way it should. As at first takes the listener back to the Torah's picture of judges: when Moses is worn out from judging everyone himself, his father-in-law Jethro tells him to find capable people, who fear God, who love truth and hate unjust gain. Notice what sits inside a blessing about justice: kindness and compassion. The blessing doesn't set justice and mercy against each other. It asks for both from the same throne. It ends with two words that often travel together in the Bible: tzedakah, righteousness, and mishpat, justice. And during the ten days from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur, the ending changes to the King of judgment, because that's the season Jews picture God judging the world. Even the prayer for fair leaders bends with the calendar.
screen: `RESTORE OUR JUDGES AS AT FIRST.` · `JETHRO: PEOPLE WHO HATE UNJUST GAIN.` · `JUSTICE WITH KINDNESS AND COMPASSION.` · `TZEDAKAH AND MISHPAT.` · then, large: `RESTORE JUSTICE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for fair leaders. Settle, and breathe. Think of the people who make decisions over your life: a judge, a mayor, a principal, a manager, a landlord, a referee. Pick one. Picture them on an ordinary day, with a hard decision on their desk. Hold one wish for them: that they see clearly, that they can't be bought, that they're kind to the person with the least power in the room. If you pray, you can ask it. The bell holds the time.
Restore justice. Hashivah shofteinu. The Amidah's eleventh blessing: return our judges as at first, with kindness and compassion.

Your line: restore justice. A week of requests: bring us back, forgive us, see our trouble, heal us, bless the year, gather the scattered, and now fair judges. Today, in one small decision you make about someone else, be the fair judge. Day five hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Hashivah shofteinu is the eleventh blessing of the weekday Amidah; during the Ten Days of Repentance its closing changes from the King who loves righteousness and justice to the King of judgment.

fork.setup: you're Moses. people line up from morning to evening for you to judge every case. what does Jethro tell you to do?
options: keep going; only you can do it.
find capable, honest people who hate unjust gain to judge with you.
fork.reveal: Jethro tells him to share the work with capable people who fear God, love truth and hate unjust gain.

original.note: Hebrew: restore our judges. the opening of the eleventh blessing, from Isaiah 1:26.

trapdoor: what you thought: a prayer about ancient courts.
what it means: a prayer for the places we go when things go wrong to work fairly, with kindness and compassion.
what a scholar hears: Isaiah 1:26 adapted; Exodus 18:21 behind as at first; hamelech hamishpat in the Ten Days of Repentance (Berakhot 12b).
